Hook.voiceover: We will evaluate it carefully is not a plan. A plan says what you measure, on which data, against which number, at which moment, and who decides what happens next.
Hook.on_screen_text: What, which data, which number, when, who

Explain.voiceover: Last time, you wrote the product sections of your PRD. Today is capstone step two. Your evaluation plan turns the metric tree and the test set into a schedule of decisions. It has five parts.

slide.title: Writing the Evaluation Plan
slide.body: AI Product Management · Lesson 14 of 15 · Capstone step 2

Explain.voiceover: First, test set design: its size, the case types and their shares, who writes the expected behaviour, and how the set is updated. Add new cases from real failures after launch, but keep a fixed core set, so results stay comparable over time.

slide.title: 1. Test set design
slide.body: Size · Case types and shares · Who writes expected behaviour · How it is updated: add real failures, keep a fixed core set

Explain.voiceover: Second, the rubric and rating method. Define each score with an example. Humans are the reference. If you use an LLM as judge, write a spot check rule, such as humans rate at least twenty percent of judge scored cases, and every case in a weak language.

slide.title: 2. Rubric and rating method
slide.body: Each score defined with an example · Humans are the reference · LLM-as-judge with a spot-check rule (e.g. humans rate ≥ 20% of judged cases + every weak-language case)

Explain.voiceover: Third, metrics and thresholds. Each metric gets a pass threshold, good enough to continue. Critical metrics also get a fail threshold that means stop or roll back. Set them before you see results. Critical failures, such as invented refunds or exposed personal data, usually have a threshold of zero.

slide.title: 3. Metrics and thresholds
slide.body: Pass threshold: good enough to continue. Fail threshold (critical metrics): stop or roll back. Critical failures (invented refunds, exposed personal data): zero tolerance. Set before results.

Explain.voiceover: Fourth, three evaluation moments. Before launch, the test set must pass before any user sees the feature. During the pilot, online metrics against a baseline, and weekly human review. After launch, a dashboard, regular sample reviews and test set reruns after every change. Fifth, a review schedule, with who decides to continue, fix or stop.

slide.title: 4. Three moments · 5. Review schedule
slide.body: Timeline: Before launch (test set must pass) → Pilot (online metrics vs baseline, weekly human review) → After launch (dashboard, sample reviews, reruns after every change). Below: review owners decide continue · fix · stop.

Explain.voiceover: Think of the inspection schedule for a new bridge. Engineers test the design before building, and the structure before opening. They inspect it on a fixed schedule after opening, with clear limits that close the bridge. Nobody decides the limits after seeing the cracks.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see an example. Dewi Lestari is a PM at a hypothetical telecom company in Indonesia. Her feature drafts replies for support agents answering messages about data packages, billing and network problems. Agents edit and send each draft.
Demonstrate.stock_query: call center agent reading customer message

Demonstrate.voiceover: Her test set has one hundred and fifty invented cases: seventy common, thirty edge, thirty split between formal Indonesian, informal Indonesian and English, and twenty that should refuse or redirect. Two senior agents write the expected behaviour. New failure cases are added every month, but the core one hundred and fifty stay fixed.

slide.title: Dewi's test set: 150 cases
slide.body: Bar split: 70 common · 30 edge (e.g. two SIM cards) · 30 language (formal Indonesian, informal Indonesian, English) · 20 refuse or redirect. Note: core 150 fixed; new failure cases added monthly.

Demonstrate.voiceover: An LLM judge scores the full set after each change. Senior agents rate a random thirty of those cases, plus every informal language case and every refusal case.

slide.title: Rating method
slide.body: Rubric: 2 correct and follows policy · 1 needs editing · 0 wrong, invents an offer or refund, or answers when it should redirect · LLM judge scores all cases · Humans rate a random 30 + every informal-language and refusal case

Demonstrate.voiceover: Before launch, the whole set must pass at eighty percent or more, and falling below seventy percent means stop. Each language group must reach seventy five percent, with a stop below sixty five. Invented offers or refunds must be zero, and all twenty refusal cases must redirect correctly.

slide.title: Thresholds before launch
slide.body: Table Metric · Pass · Fail (stop): Pass rate, whole set · ≥ 80% · < 70% | Pass rate, each language group · ≥ 75% · < 65% | Invented offers or refunds · 0 · any | Correct redirects on refusal cases · all 20 · any answered

Demonstrate.voiceover: During the pilot, more than half of drafts should be sent with light or no editing by week four. Handling time must beat the baseline, and the complaint re open rate must not stay above it for two weeks. Dewi and the operations lead meet every two weeks to decide, and the operations lead owns the kill switch.

slide.title: Pilot thresholds and reviews
slide.body: Drafts sent with light or no editing > 50% by week 4 · Handling time below baseline (stop if above for 2 weeks) · Re-open rate not above baseline (stop if above for 2 weeks). Reviews: ML engineer after every change · 50 drafts weekly · decision meeting every 2 weeks · kill switch: operations lead.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is setting thresholds only for the overall pass rate. A feature can pass overall, while failing a whole language group.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, an evaluation plan covers test set design, the rubric and rating method, metrics with thresholds, three evaluation moments and a review schedule with owners. Second, set pass and fail thresholds before seeing results, for each user group, with zero tolerance for critical failures. Third, evaluation continues after launch.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Five parts of an evaluation plan. 2. Pass and fail thresholds set first, per group, zero tolerance for critical failures. 3. Evaluation continues after launch.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. This is capstone step two. In the exercise below, write your evaluation plan, with your test set design, rubric, a threshold table of at least six metrics, and a review schedule. Start from your twenty cases from lesson nine. It takes about forty five minutes. In the final lesson, we review and present your PRD. See you there.
